translationRepairs: In the eighth month he drove the rebels to Altishahr and then to Lake Yashilkul, where the Muslim communities submitted.
In the eighth month he drove the rebels to Alchur and then to Lake Yashilkul, where the Muslim communities submitted.
The source names 阿勒楚爾, the specific place Alchur; Altishahr is a different, broader toponym.
In the eighth month he pursued the rebels to Altishahr and then to Lake Yashilkul; the Muslim populace submitted.
In the eighth month he pursued the rebels to Alchur and then to Lake Yashilkul; the Muslim populace submitted.
The literal field has the same toponym error: 阿勒楚爾 is Alchur, not Altishahr.
He proposed garrison colonies at Manas, Kur, Karasu, and Jinghe, with fifteen mu allotted to each settler.
He proposed garrison colonies at Manas-Kur, Karasu, and Jinghe, with fifteen mu allotted to each settler.
三地 explicitly counts three sites, so 瑪納斯庫爾 is one compound toponym; splitting it creates an impossible fourth site.
He memorialized on garrison farming at Manas, Kur, Karasu, and Jinghe, allotting fifteen mu per person.
He memorialized on garrison farming at Manas-Kur, Karasu, and Jinghe, allotting fifteen mu per person.
The literal field must likewise preserve the three-place count by rendering 瑪納斯庫爾 as one name.
The emperor blamed them for the delay, saying it had shown weakness and cost imperial prestige; although the ministry recommended dismissal, he kept them in office and stationed A Gui at Yarkand.
The emperor blamed them for the delay, saying it had shown weakness and cost imperial prestige; although the ministry recommended dismissal, he kept them in office and stationed A Gui at Yar.
雅爾城 denotes Yar, not Yarkand (葉爾羌); the proposal restores the actual place of posting.

The emperor rebuked them for delay, saying it showed cowardice and damaged prestige; the ministry proposed stripping them of office, but the emperor ordered them to remain in post and garrison Yarkand.
The emperor rebuked them for delay, saying it showed cowardice and damaged prestige; the ministry proposed stripping them of office, but the emperor ordered them to remain in post and garrison Yar.
The literal field also misidentifies 雅爾城 as Yarkand; Yar is the supported place-name.
A Gui proposed relocating the Yarkand garrison to Chuchu, and the court approved.
A Gui proposed relocating the Yar garrison city to Chuchu, and the court approved.
The memorial concerns moving 雅爾城, Yar city, to Chuchu; Yarkand is not named here.
A Gui memorialized to move Yarkand to Chuchu, and the request was granted.
A Gui memorialized to move Yar city to Chuchu, and the request was granted.
The literal replacement correctly identifies 雅爾城 as Yar city and retains the relocation to Chuchu.
He asked that three courier stations be established from Chuchu to Urtubulak to open communications with Yarkand, and the ministries were ordered to carry this out.
He asked that three courier stations be established from Chuchu to Urtubulak to open communications with Yar, and the ministries were ordered to carry this out.
The courier stations were intended to connect with 雅爾, Yar; replacing Yarkand corrects the route without altering the sentence.
He requested that three courier stations be set up from Chuchu to Urtubulak to link with Yarkand; the matter was referred to the relevant ministry for implementation.
He requested that three courier stations be set up from Chuchu to Urtubulak to link with Yar; the matter was referred to the relevant ministry for implementation.
The literal field has the same place-name error; 以通雅爾 means establishing a link with Yar.

By then the Jinchuan chieftain Langka was dead, but his son Sonom and Zewang's son Senggesang of Lesser Jinchuan were raiding the frontier; Governor-General Ertai's campaign had failed, and the emperor ordered A Gui to join Deputy Commander Wenfu in the advance.

By then the Jinchuan chieftain Langka was dead, but his son Sonom and Zewang's son Senggesang of Lesser Jinchuan were raiding the frontier; Governor-General Altai's campaign had failed, and the emperor ordered A Gui to join Deputy Commander Wenfu in the advance.
阿爾泰 is Altai; Ertai suggests the distinct Qing official Ortai (鄂爾泰). The proposal correctly repairs the personal name.

At that time the Jinchuan chieftain Langka was already dead; his son Sonom and the Lesser Jinchuan chieftain Zewang's son Senggesang were harassing the border; Sichuan governor-general Ertai campaigned against them without success, and the emperor ordered A Gui to follow Deputy Commander and Minister Wenfu in the advance.

At that time the Jinchuan chieftain Langka was already dead; his son Sonom and the Lesser Jinchuan chieftain Zewang's son Senggesang were harassing the border; Sichuan governor-general Altai campaigned against them without success, and the emperor ordered A Gui to follow Deputy Commander and Minister Wenfu in the advance.
The literal field names the same 四川總督阿爾泰; Altai is the accurate rendering here.

Vice Minister Guilin had replaced Ertai as governor-general and led his troops to Molong Ravine, where they were beaten and Vice Commander Xue Cong was killed; Ertai impeached Guilin and had him removed.

Vice Minister Guilin had replaced Altai as governor-general and led his troops to Molong Ravine, where they were beaten and Vice Commander Xue Cong was killed; Altai impeached Guilin and had him removed.
Both references are to Altai (阿爾泰), first as Guilin's predecessor and then as Guilin's accuser.

At that time Vice Minister Guilin replaced Ertai as governor-general and also took over his forces; reaching Molong Ravine, he met defeat and Vice Commander Xue Cong was killed; Ertai impeached and had Guilin dismissed.

At that time Vice Minister Guilin replaced Altai as governor-general and also took over his forces; reaching Molong Ravine, he met defeat and Vice Commander Xue Cong was killed; Altai impeached and had Guilin dismissed.
The literal field contains the same two mistaken instances of Ertai; the proposed Altai corrections are accurate.

Following the tribal guide Mutar, they split the force along central and southern routes while secretly posting men on the northern ridge, then seized Meinuo. Mingliang's column also took Sengge Stockade and linked up. Within seven days, Lesser Jinchuan was subdued.

Following a strategy proposed by Mutar, a local tribesman, they split the force along the central and southern routes while secretly sending troops to the northern summit, then seized Meinuo. Mingliang's column also took Sengge Stockade and linked up. Within seven days, Lesser Jinchuan was subdued.
策 makes Mutar the source of the strategy, not a guide. The proposal fixes that error but 'tribal native' is awkward, so the revision renders 番人 naturally as 'local tribesman.'
Meanwhile Fengsheng'e was moving along the northern route; when his column reached Kailiye and saw the beacon fires, he knew the main army was coming to link up.
Meanwhile Fengsheng'e was moving along the northern route; when his column reached Kailiye and saw the beacon fires, he brought his army to join them.
以師來會 makes Fengsheng'e the agent who brings his force to the rendezvous; the original reverses that movement.
At this time Fengsheng'e was advancing from the northern route; when his army reached Kailiye and saw signal fires, he knew the main force had come to join him.
At this time Fengsheng'e was advancing from the northern route; when his army reached Kailiye and saw signal fires, he came with his army to join them.
The literal proposal correctly restores Fengsheng'e as the one who came with his army to join the others.

In the forty-second year the acting Yunnan-Guizhou governor Tusi De memorialized: "Meng Bo is dead; his son Zhuajiaoya has succeeded, professes loyalty, offers tribute, and wishes to return to Chinese rule.

In the forty-second year, acting Yunnan-Guizhou governor-general Tuside memorialized: "Meng Bo has died. His son Zhuajiaoya has succeeded him, professed allegiance, offered tribute, and is willing to return Chinese subjects.
圖思德 is the single name Tuside, while 歸中國人 is transitive: Zhuajiaoya is willing to return Chinese subjects, not submit to Chinese rule. The revision also regularizes the report's title and tense.
Zhejiang financial commissioner Sheng Zhu reported that Governor Chen Huizu was privately tied to the family of Wang Tanwang; the emperor ordered A Gui to Zhejiang to investigate.

Zhejiang financial commissioner Sheng Zhu reported that Governor Chen Huizu had privately appropriated property while confiscating the household of Wang Tanwang; the emperor ordered A Gui to Zhejiang to investigate.
籍王亶望家 means confiscating Wang Tanwang's household or estate, and 有所私 indicates private appropriation, not a personal family tie.
Zhejiang financial commissioner Sheng Zhu memorialized that Governor Chen Huizu had private ties to the family of Wang Tanwang; the emperor ordered A Gui to go to Zhejiang to investigate.

Zhejiang financial commissioner Sheng Zhu memorialized that Governor Chen Huizu had privately appropriated something while confiscating Wang Tanwang's household; the emperor ordered A Gui to go to Zhejiang to investigate.
The literal proposal accurately makes the charge an improper taking during confiscation rather than invented private ties to Wang's family.
At dusk his generals urged him: "We must seize Sonom tonight, or he may yet slip away."
At dusk his generals urged him: "We must take Sonom alive today, or something else may happen."
今日 is 'today,' 生致 is to take alive, and 慮有他 leaves the feared alternative unspecified; the proposal restores each point.
A Gui had his escort dismount, hung their cloaks on the trees to resemble additional troops, remounted, and rode slowly down the slope.
A Gui ordered all his horsemen to dismount, remove their garments, tear them into pieces, and hang the pieces from the trees; then he ordered them to remount and descend the knoll slowly.
The original invents cloaks and states the purpose prematurely. The proposal removes those additions but omits 裂, so the revision explicitly includes tearing the garments before hanging them.
